title: 2035 came early
author: setheron
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009
I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

comments.author: gbl08ma
comments.textRawHtml: I had been working (read: prompting Claude) on https://waarm64.com for two months and it was slightly heartbreaking to see unkernel get all the attention when I was like two weeks away from a public announcement. It would obviously have been worse if I had actually built more of mine "by hand," but still, even if just doing by orchestration/"asking good questions to the LLM" kind of work, I spent probably over a hundred hours on it. I rushed its release, but now I don't even really feel like working much more on mine anymore, even though it achieves (or achieved) better performance than unkernel and (for now) still has a more complete feature set. Oh well, it is in line with the motivation I had for mine, which was to see if LLMs could help one person build that sort of thing. Turns out that not only can LLMs do the bulk of this kind of work, they can do it so well that numerous projects of the same kind are popping up pretty much simultaneously. They still can't make WebAssembly beat hardware virtualization, though :D

children.author: sneurlax
children.textRawHtml:
Similar occurred to me recently: in June I got Airdrop working between Apple and non-Apple devices with a Rust crate “awdl”. Months later, someone else made owly and got 3,000 stars

But I got just a little bit more working such that I was able to upstream a few PRs their way. Now I don’t have to maintain an unwieldy codebase alone while being able to still enjoy actually using the functionality and wrapping it for other consumers (Dart, Flutter).

An independent implementation is sometimes very valuable for the next reader’s study and for the health of the wider ecosystem. Keep at it or at least share where you stopped—-don’t hoard until you have something perfect.

children.author: gbl08ma
children.textRawHtml: What use cases do you have in mind for Vulkan on WebGPU? That adapter is the trickiest one to fully complete (there are many things Vulkan allows and WebGPU simply doesn't, and that can't be converted/emulated in a performant way) and I've lost some of the motivation for continuing to work on it, because I'm finding it tricky to find software that takes advantage of Vulkan while simultaneously being sufficiently light on CPU to run well within waarm64 (and also while being aarch64-native, because while FEX works, it makes the CPU performance story even worse). The Godot editor, and any projects I can compile through it, have been the main driver so far, with its Forward+ renderer.

children.author: gbl08ma
children.textRawHtml:
Elsewhere in these comments someone shared another initiative that seems very close to this: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50626676

I think that software compatibility with these kinds of solutions will always be worse than emulating an entire machine, even if performance has some opportunities to be better (and for some software, it'll be _much_ better to compile directly to wasm). For one, wasm is still a bit of a niche target for many compilers; working on waarm64 alone, Claude found a wasm miscompile in Rust that turned out to be a LLVM problem (which I already reported and has already been fixed upstream). Then there's all the closed source software: it's probably a far fetched example in terms of use cases, but good luck getting e.g. Valve/Steam to care about wasm when they've only started caring about aarch64 recently - meanwhile, Steam already works, with some patience, in my emulator.

children.author: gbl08ma
children.textRawHtml:
That part is not LLM authored. I should have given up on making a bit of a play on words, and I'm yet to fix it. It is meant to be a reference to how, depending on how "AI" evolves, it can either be very positive for individual freedoms, or end up limiting them in some senses. If some doomsday predictions of "AI replaces all knowledge work" become reality, then it will have (de)valued much of human skill. It is also possible that the powers that be will determine that it is giving ordinary people too many capabilities, and that connects with the window of capability eventually closing. I hope that was clear enough.

In general Opus and Fable are terrible at writing English, even for UI elements, compared to their software development abilities, and this is even after setting rules for what the copy should be like. I've been slowly going through all of the user-visible text in the project to make it read better, but it's funny that my own writing has defects too. It's definitely not great to have to read Opus writing every day.
